title: A steam locomotive anime short
title_zh: 蒸汽机车动漫短片
author: 0kncn
prompt:
Create a 2D anime short. It must look completely like real Japanese anime, as if it were taken directly from a finished theatrical anime film. This is traditional-looking, hand-drawn 2D anime, not a 3D animation, a moving illustration, or a stylized web graphic.

Build everything in Blender from Python, render it in Eevee, then ink and paint every frame in a second pass. Deliver one 1920x1080, 24 fps MP4 with a synthesized soundtrack. Use any tools, libraries, references, guides, literally anything, as long as the final result looks 100% like hand-drawn 2D anime.

Use theatrical anime as the art style reference for the design, line work, painted backgrounds, color and atmosphere. The film is 90 seconds long (2160 frames), in 42 shots. Its hero is a steam locomotive that transforms into a robot. No people appear in the film.

HERO
No. 9, a 1940s 2-8-2 freight locomotive with a four-axle tender, 23 m long, asleep for decades in a mountain engine shed: matte black boiler with rust runs, faded red wheel centres and buffer beam, brass number plate "9", one large headlamp, two amber marker lamps, moss on the running boards, ivy through the cab windows, and a stork's nest on the cab roof. As a robot it stands 21 m tall with its shoulders at 17 m. It is an original design, not a character from any existing series. It moves on twos, slow and heavy. Its wheels never slip and its feet never slide.

TRANSFORM
One transformation, at full speed, 120 frames, in five stages of 24 frames. Every part is rigid: nothing stretches, nothing vanishes, nothing appears. Each part travels on a hinge or a slide you can see.
1. Legs: the tender uncouples, splits lengthwise and swings down; its two bogies lock as feet, the coal stays in bunkers on the calves.
2. Hips: the cab drops and widens into the pelvis; the trailing truck folds onto the lower back.
3. Torso: the boiler tilts upright, firebox at the waist, smokebox at the top; the chimney and steam dome end on the upper back and keep venting.
4. Arms: the running boards swing out with the cylinders as shoulders, the piston and connecting rods as forearms, and hands with three fingers and a thumb unfolding from the valve gear; the front driving wheels ride up as shoulder discs, the rear ones fold to hips and knees.
5. Head: the smokebox door hinges forward as the chest plate with the headlamp at its centre; a riveted helmet rises from the smokebox with one dark visor slit and the two marker lamps as amber eyes; the cowcatcher folds up as a collar.
The cab roof panel rides up to the right shoulder and carries the stork's nest, never tilted more than 10 degrees.
Stages 1-3 happen on the rails, with the first strides landing on the ballast either side of the track. Stages 4-5 happen in the air.

WORLD
A single-track mountain railway at real scale. At the top, an ore mine with a loading bunker and a rake of twelve four-wheel hopper wagons. The line descends through larch forest and a short rock tunnel to a viaduct: seven 18 m steel girder spans on stone piers, 126 m long, the deck 17 m above a turquoise meltwater river 3 m deep. Beyond it, a small station: a stone engine shed, a water tower, a semaphore signal with an alarm bell, a signal box, a siding ending in a sand drag. Snow peaks behind, a cliff face above the viaduct, telegraph poles along the whole line.

STORY
A clear spring morning in the valley. Meltwater loosens the cliff: a rockfall hits the middle pier of the viaduct, the pier collapses into the river and the two girders it carried sag into a V, held only by the rails. Up at the mine the shock snaps a coupling and the twelve loaded wagons start to roll downhill, unmanned. At the station the semaphore drops to danger and the bell rings. In the dark shed the firebox glows, the pressure needle climbs, the headlamp lights; the stork flies up. No. 9 bursts through the shed doors tearing ivy and rust, and charges up the grade with the wagons coming down the other side. On the approach it transforms at full speed, leaps from the abutment, lands crouched in the river, wades to the fallen pier, and lifts the sagging joint onto its shoulders and raised hands. The wagons hit the viaduct: it sinks 0.3 m as each one passes over and holds. The rake runs through the station into the sand drag and stops. No. 9 does not come back out. It locks its knees and stays as the new pier. The steam thins, the stork returns to its nest, the visor dims.

LIGHT
High-key anime light, never murky: a morning sun from the south-east, a saturated cobalt sky, white cumulus with lavender shadows, snow peaks with blue shadows, fresh green larch, a turquoise river with drawn white water. Light only changes with a cause you can see: rock dust dims the gorge for 3 seconds, steam whites out a frame, the firebox throws orange onto the shed walls. Cel light with hard shadows, gouache backgrounds, ink lines on every machine, rail and building, effects drawn on twos: steam as inked rolling shapes with a flat shadow tone, water as inked sheets with foam crowns, dust as drawn clouds, never particle mush.

SOUND
A synthesized orchestra on a 144 bpm grid: one beat is 10 frames, and every cut lands on a multiple of 5 frames. A hopeful theme on clarinet and horn, the collapse in E minor, a 12/8 chase with the exhaust chuff as percussion at four beats per wheel revolution, a heavy 3/4 for the hold with one low drum per wagon. 16 hits land exactly on the picture: the rockfall, the pier, the coupling, the signal arm, the shed doors, each transformation lock, the landing, the lift, the first and last wagon. The steam whistle is heard twice: once on waking, once on the hold.

FORMAT
Write the film as a Python story clock: one state per frame for every pose, camera, wheel angle, rod position, transformation part, wagon, effect and sound cue.

CHECKS
Before the final render a script tests every frame on the real meshes: no part of No. 9 goes through another part, in either form or at any frame of the transformation; the total volume of its parts is the same in both forms; every wheel on a rail turns exactly as far as it travels; planted feet do not move; No. 9 never goes through the track, the shed, the viaduct or the riverbed; the wagons stay on the rails and never touch each other except at the couplings; the camera never enters a mesh, the cliff or the water; nothing jumps between frames.

title: A zombie eagle sculpted through Blender MCP
title_zh: 用 Blender MCP 雕出的僵尸鹰
author: maxt3chno
prompt:
You are building a game-ready 3D creature in Blender through Blender MCP (execute_blender_code for actions, renders and viewport screenshots to check your work). The attached image is the reference. Goal: an outstanding, realistic, production-quality model that matches the reference as closely as possible. Work like a senior creature artist: plan, build, look at your renders critically, fix, and only move on when a stage really looks right. Never ask me questions; if something is unclear, choose the option closest to the reference and continue.

WORK_DIR = C:\Users\Max\Documents\Claude\Fablr (create subfolders textures, renders, export). Save after every stage as WORK_DIR\eagle_stage#.blend. Work only inside WORK_DIR. If Blender is not running, start "C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation\Blender 5.2\blender.exe" --online-mode yourself; the MCP add-on starts on port 9876.

========================================
WHAT IT IS
A zombie war eagle from a dark, gritty survival island game: a huge, ragged, half-dead bird of prey standing on the ground, hunched forward, wings half-open and drooping, screaming, ready to attack. Realistic, heavy, dirty, dangerous. Never cartoon, never toy-like.
Size: about 1.6 m tall hunched (top of the head about 1.45 m), wingspan about 4.2 m in this pose.
Metres. Faces -Y, Z up, feet on the ground at Z = 0, origin between the feet.
Static model in the pose of the reference. No rig, no animation.
========================================
THE REFERENCE, PART BY PART
HEAD AND SKULLReal eagle/vulture skull shape: flat top, heavy bony brow ridge, long face running into the beak, cheek and jaw lines readable under the feathers. Pushed forward and slightly down, angry.
Head and neck feathers: pale grey-beige, shaggy, messy, spiky on top and at the back of the head, darker and dirtier toward the neck.

BEAK AND MOUTHBig raptor beak: deep at the base, curving down into a sharp hook that overhangs the lower beak, sharp cutting edges, cere with nostril at the base. Grey-yellow horn, darker and dirty toward the tip, small chips and cracks.
Separate lower beak, mouth wide open (about 35-40 degrees), pink-red tongue, dark wet throat.

EYESSet deep in the sockets under the brow ridge, only part of the eyeball visible, real eyelids around them.
Its RIGHT eye (left side of the image): blind, milky white with a faint grey iris shadow. A deep diagonal scar runs through it from the forehead to the cheek: a real cut in the geometry, feathers missing along it, dried dark red blood.
Its LEFT eye (right side of the image): amber-orange iris with a darker outer ring, round black pupil, glossy cornea, faint glow.

BODYThick, heavy chest and shoulders, dark brown-black feathers, wet and clumped, layered down the body.
Long shaggy feathers hang from the belly and thighs like a torn skirt, uneven, some broken.

WOUNDOn its LEFT shoulder (right side of the image), where the wing meets the body: a torn hole in the skin. Ragged skin edge with feathers pulled out around it, lumpy wet dark-red flesh going inward.
Two broken bones coming out of the flesh (one pointing up, one sideways), off-white to yellow, jagged splintered ends, a bit of blood on them.

WINGSHalf-open and drooping: shoulders high, elbows out and slightly forward, wrists low, long primaries hanging down and outward, tips almost on the ground. Real wing anatomy: shoulder, elbow, wrist.
Layered feathers: small and medium coverts over the top, secondaries along the arm, long primaries at the hand.
Colours: black, dark brown, rust-orange, with light/dark bars across many feathers. Many feathers are torn, split, broken or missing, leaving gaps.

NATURAL LEG: its right leg (left side of the image)Thigh hidden in feathers, then a thick scaly tarsus: big overlapping scutes on the front, small pebbly scales on the sides, yellow-brown, dirty, cracked.
Foot: 3 toes forward, 1 back, thick toe pads, long black curved talons with sharp tips.

MECHANICAL LEG: its left leg (right side of the image)A crude, heavy prosthetic of rusty dark iron, as thick as the real leg or thicker, hand-made from scrap.
Upper part: thick pipe with bolted plates, round knee hub with a big bolt, a rod or piston along the back.
Lower part wrapped in dirty leather straps and rags with blood stains, wire or rope tied around them.
Iron foot with 3 forward and 1 back hinged claw blades: thick, hooked, chipped, rusty, dried blood.
The top is strapped into the torn, bloody flesh of the thigh.

========================================
HOW TO BUILD IT
BLOCKOUT. Simple shapes in the exact hunched pose. Front camera (orthographic) with the reference as background; also side and 3/4 cameras. Match proportions and pose to the reference before any detail. This is the most important check.
BODY MESH. One clean, subdivision-ready quad mesh for body, neck, head and natural leg, with edge loops around eyes, beak, shoulders, wing roots and joints. Sculpt the skull, brow, cheeks, beak base and leg scales (multires or a displacement map from your own height map).
FEATHERS. This decides the whole look, so give it the most care.Feather atlas, 2048 px: draw 10-16 different feathers yourself in numpy. Each one has a vane outline (tapered, slightly asymmetric), a central shaft (rachis), fine barb lines angled off the shaft, a few splits and gaps in the vane, a broken or ragged tip on some. Colour variants: black, dark brown, rust, barred (light/dark stripes), pale beige for the head. Alpha mask, plus a normal map from the barb lines and roughness.
Cards: every card shows exactly ONE whole feather from ONE atlas cell, with UVs fitted to that cell. Never tile the atlas across a card. Material with alpha (Alpha Clip about 0.5, or Alpha Hashed), backface culling off, light passing slightly through (translucency or a little subsurface).
Each card is curved: a slight bend along the shaft and across the vane, never a flat plane.
Placement: scatter by script along the surface, oriented to a flow direction (from head toward tail and down the limbs), in overlapping rows like roof tiles. Random size, rotation, curl and colour within limits. Clumps of 3-5 feathers stuck together where it is wet. Head and neck feathers short and spiky, chest feathers medium and layered, belly and thigh fringe long and hanging.
Wings: primaries and secondaries are real thin meshes (vane with slight thickness and a raised shaft), fanned from the wrist and the arm, each with its own angle and droop, some torn or missing. Coverts as layered cards over them.
Under the feather cards, the body mesh is dark brown so gaps never show bright skin.

WOUND. Cut a real hole in the body mesh at the shoulder, model the ragged skin edge as a thin flap, fill the hole with lumpy flesh going inward, add the two broken bones from cylinders with splintered, displaced ends.
NATURAL LEG. Scutes and scales as real relief, toe pads, 4 talons as separate curved hard meshes.
MECHANICAL LEG. Hard-surface modelling: pipes, plates, bolts, knee hub, piston, straps, rag wraps (cloth with thickness and folds), wire, hinged claw blades. Bevel all metal edges so they catch the light.
MATERIALS (PBR, own textures, 2048 px max per set):Feathers: from the atlas, darker and wet at the roots, slightly lighter worn edges, dirt.
Beak: grey-yellow horn, darker tip, dirt in the cracks. Mouth and tongue wet pink-red, throat dark.
Eyes: glossy cornea; one milky blind, one amber with a faint glow.
Flesh: wet dark red with lighter and darker patches. Dried blood dark brown-red, matte. Bones off-white to yellow, slightly glossy.
Natural leg: yellow-brown scales, dark dirt in the gaps, black glossy talons.
Prosthetic: dark rusty iron, bright worn metal on edges and bolt heads, orange-brown rust in recesses, brown leather, dirty grey-brown bloody rags.

========================================
CHECKS
After each build step render front, 3/4 and side views (EEVEE, studio light from the upper left, neutral grey background). Put the front render next to the reference and look critically. Fix what is clearly off before moving on.
At the end also render: head close-up, both feet close-up, wound close-up, one wing from behind.
Final self-check, all must be true:
Silhouette and pose match the reference.
Feathers read as soft, individual, layered feathers with barbs and ragged edges, never as hard plates, combs or a repeating pattern.
The beak is a hooked raptor beak, wide open, tongue visible.
The eyes sit deep under the brow; one blind and scarred, one amber.
Wound and bones read clearly; prosthetic is heavy, rusty and crude.
No holes, no floating parts, no feather card seen edge-on as a thin line, no bad intersections.
========================================
GAME LIMITS
At most 80,000 triangles total, feather cards included.
At most 4 texture sets, each at most 2048 x 2048. In the GLB use JPEG for colour maps and PNG only where alpha is needed; the GLB should be under 30 MB.
Object names: eagle_body, eagle_feathers, eagle_wings, eagle_beak, eagle_eyes, eagle_wound, eagle_prosthetic.
========================================
OUTPUT
WORK_DIR\export\eagle.glb (textures embedded) and WORK_DIR\export\eagle.blend.
WORK_DIR\export\final_front.png, final_34.png, final_side.png, final_head.png, final_feet.png, final_compare.png (reference next to final front).
A short report: triangle count, texture sets and sizes, GLB size.

title: A rigged zombie hand that crawls and backflips
title_zh: 会爬会后空翻的绑定僵尸手
author: higgsfield_ai
prompt:
Using Blender's Python API (bpy, bmesh, mathutils), build a complete animation pipeline from scratch and get it right on the first pass:

1. Model an original stylized cartoon zombie hand with stylized wounds, stitches and a severed stump at the wrist.
2. Build a production-style rig with custom controllers (IK/FK, gizmo rings, curl sliders).
3. Animate it pose to pose first, then polish the curves (overlapping action, weight, floor contact).
4. Set up rich, tactile cartoon shading, texturing and lighting.
5. Render the final video on a cloud GPU with Higgsfield GPU (the /gpu command).

## 1. Design and modeling

Design an appealing, characterful stylized cartoon zombie hand with a cartoon game look.

1. Silhouette and proportions
   - Expressive cartoon anatomy: a broad, sculpted back of the hand, plump palm pads, slightly oversized knuckles, three clear segments on each finger and a two-segment thumb with a heavy base.
   - Faceted, stylized geometry with clearly readable finger segments and knuckles.
   - Chunky cartoon fingernails, slightly curved, with a triangular chip on one or two of them.
2. Zombie details on the back of the hand and the stump
   - Back of the hand and wrist: clean cartoon zombie details, not gory realism. Add a stylized torn wound on the back of the hand and a cut near the wrist, held shut with 2–3 large metal staples or thick cross-stitches.
   - Severed stump: a stepped cut of purple-magenta flesh with a smooth, cream-white cartoon bone sticking out of the center, ending in a rounded knob.
   - Optionally add one or two small craters or scars, or a loose bandage around the wrist, so the silhouette reads clearly from every angle.
3. Animation-ready topology
   - Put three parallel edge loops on every finger joint and across the knuckles, so the mesh doesn't collapse or break when a finger bends 90°.
   - Use Subdivision Surface with controlled creases and bevels to keep a faceted cartoon feel on smooth forms.

## 2. Rig and custom controllers

Build a full armature with clean weights (Automatic Weights, then a scripted per-segment cleanup for the finger segments, palm and stump) and visible custom controllers (custom_shape).

1. Deform bone hierarchy
   - Root: global movement and in-air rotation for the backflip.
   - Wrist_Stump and Bone_Core: stump bend and twist, plus a small independent jiggle of the bone.
   - Palm_L, Palm_Center, Palm_R: the palm arch (cupping and spreading) when the hand pushes against the floor.
   - Full chains for all five fingers: Metacarpal → Proximal_01 → Intermediate_02 → Distal_03 → Tip.
2. Controls
   - Clean, colored gizmo controllers around the finger joints and the wrist: Circle, Square and Cone meshes that don't render, assigned with pose_bone.custom_shape and colored by group (green, cyan and yellow outlines).
   - An IK/FK switch for every finger and a panel of finger-curl sliders next to the hand.
   - A Floor constraint (or a Z >= 0 check for the fingertips), so the fingers never pass through the floor while crawling or landing.

## 3. Animation: key poses first, then polish

Animate in two passes, the way professional 3D animators work.

### Pass 1: key-pose blocking

Set clear key poses with readable silhouettes and check them on the timeline (30 fps, 20 seconds / 600 frames):

- Block 1 (0:00–0:03, frames 1–90). Wake up and flex. The hand lies still, then twitches like a zombie (a quick double spasm of the pinky and index finger), clenches into a claw-like half-fist and fans its fingers wide.
- Block 2 (0:03–0:05, frames 91–150). Spider arch. The fingertips press into the ground and push the palm and the bone stump high into a springy spider arch.
- Block 3 (0:05–0:10, frames 151–300). Spider crawl. Six to eight full, coordinated steps forward on a slight curve, walking on the fingertips. The fingers move out of sync (index and ring, then middle and pinky, with the thumb steering from the side), the weight shifts, and the palm dips on every step. Planted fingertips never slide, and the stump sways behind with inertia.
- Block 4 (0:10–0:14, frames 301–420). Wind-up and backflip. A deep crouch on bent fingers (anticipation), a powerful push off the fingertips, a full 360° backflip with the fingers tucked, the palm opening just before touchdown, then a springy landing that settles (squash and settle).
- Block 5 (0:14–0:20, frames 421–600). Gesture combo.
  - The hand rises onto its wrist, snaps into a fist and fires a finger gun: the index finger shoots forward and the thumb cocks up like a hammer, two shots with recoil.
  - It opens into a wide fan and rolls on its long axis, showing the wounds and staples on the back and clean deformation on both sides.
  - It finishes on a neat OK sign (thumb and index finger form a ring, the other three fingers fan upward) and holds with a subtle breathing motion.

### Pass 2: curve polish (Graph Editor, F-curves)

After the key poses, run a script over every F-curve:

- Convert the keys to smooth AUTO_CLAMPED / BEZIER curves.
- Add overlapping action and follow-through of 2–4 frames on the fingertips (the distal segments finish bending slightly after the proximal ones) and on the stump with its bone.
- Add a slight tremor while the fingers carry weight, and a small overshoot on the fast gestures (the finger gun and the OK sign).
- Run a strict check that no finger goes through the floor.

## 4. Shading, lighting and output

1. Materials (Cycles or EEVEE Next)
   - Zombie skin: a saturated cartoon rotten-green base (#5E8C42 blending into #3D5E2A) with soft subsurface scattering (a yellow-green radius), so the fingers glow when backlit.
   - Knuckles, joints and creases: procedural darkening with a sickly plum tint (#4A2C56) in the knuckle creases, around the wounds and under the nails (Geometry → Pointiness or Ambient Occlusion, plus vertex colors or procedural masks).
   - Wounds, stump and bone: moist purple-crimson flesh in the cuts and on the stump (Roughness = 0.25), a matte cream-white bone (#E6DEC8), and metal staples with a bright highlight (Metallic = 0.9, Roughness = 0.2).
   - Nails: grimy yellowish semi-gloss keratin with a dark edge at the cuticle.
2. Lighting and set
   - A dark slate floor with a fine matte stone texture and crisp contact shadows under every finger.
   - Three-point lighting: a strong cool teal rim light from above and behind (to outline the fingers, staples and wounds), a soft warm key light at 45° and a gentle fill.
3. Output: rig and render in one video (20 seconds)
   - Show both the rig at work, in two synced Blender viewports (an isometric view and a side view on a dark background, with the controllers visible), and the final cinematic Cycles render.
   - For example: the render on one side and the two rig viewports on the other, switching to a full-screen render for the backflip and the final pose.
   - Deliver 1080×1920 (vertical) or 1920×1080 (horizontal).

The final render needs to be 1920×1080, horizontal.

## 5. Self-check and final render on Higgsfield GPU

1. Check the key poses locally
   - Before rendering the whole animation, render 6 check frames locally: (1) the back of the hand with the wounds and the bone, (2) the spider arch, (3) a crawl step, (4) the backflip in mid-air, (5) the finger gun, (6) the OK sign with the rig controllers visible.
   - Review every frame yourself: no finger twisted at an unnatural angle, no torn mesh, wounds and staples sitting tight on the skin, and a zombie shader that looks rich and stylized.
2. Final render on Higgsfield GPU
   - Use the /gpu command from the Higgsfield MCP. List the GPUs and their prices, and check that nothing of mine is already running.
   - Quote the render job, upload the .blend file to it, then show me the GPU, the expected credits and the most it can cost. Start only after my yes.
   - Render the full animation in Cycles at high quality with GPU denoising (OptiX or OIDN). Export the final .mp4 (H.264, -crf 15) and download the video and the .blend file.
   - Follow the job until it ends. Don't give up on errors or timeouts: keep going until there's a finished video file.

prompt:
Task: turn the robot head model you built into a 30-second product launch film in Blender (bpy), with a mechanical rig, an inside-out assembly and a final Cycles render on Higgsfield GPU.

1. Mechanical rig (Armature + Constraints + Drivers). Rigid parts move on joints, no smooth skinning:

- Neck: three-axis kinematics (Neck_Base, Neck_Mid, Head_Pivot). The hydraulic pistons slide in and out of their cylinders as the head tilts; the colored cable bundles flex slightly but stay under their ties.

- Jaw: the pink jaw and the lower teeth hinge on Jaw_Bone; the side rods and rear dampers move in sync.

- Eyes: both lenses aim at a shared target (Eye_LookAt_Target) with micro-saccades; the focus rings turn and the aperture opens and closes.

- Temple gears turn with the head and the jaw (Driver); the indicators pulse.

- Exploded-view assembly rig for every layer: neck → skull frame → temple gears → eyes → cables → jaw and teeth → blue shell panels → screws.

2. Script: 30 seconds, 30 fps (900 frames), 16:9. Bezier curves with ease-in/ease-out and a slight overshoot when parts lock into place.

Act I, The Assembly (0–15 s):

- 0–4 s: macro low-angle shot; the neck column, pistons and cables snap into place.

- 4–8 s: 3/4 orbit; the skull frame, temple gears and lens eyes assemble.

- 8–11 s: close-up; the pink jaw locks on and the colored teeth drop in as a cascade.

- 11–15 s: the blue shell panels close in from an exploded view; screws spin in, the last one at 14.5 s.

Act II, The Awakening (15–30 s):

- 15–19 s: the indicators light up, the eyes focus and look into the camera.

- 19–23 s: side and rear tracking; the head turns and tilts, and the gears, pistons and cables work through the shell.

- 23–26.5 s: the jaw opens and runs a series of articulation moves.

- 26.5–30 s: hero shot, slow push-out; the jaw closes, the eyes make a final micro-focus, a rim light sweeps across the shell.

3. Look (Cycles): a seamless grey-to-graphite studio, an overhead softbox, two rim lights shining through the translucent shell and an eye catchlight. Motion blur (shutter 0.5), animated depth of field, a subtle glare on the indicators, AgX Medium High Contrast.

4. Render: debug locally and check 8 test stills, one per shot: nothing falls apart, the eyes and teeth move with the skull and jaw, glass and metal look photoreal. Then render all 900 frames in Cycles with GPU denoising on Higgsfield GPU with /gpu: show me the price first and start only after my yes. When it's done, download the .mp4 and the .blend.

title: A volume slider with an underwater world
title_zh: 装着海底世界的音量滑块
author: N1njaCodex
prompt:
Make "Deep Dive Switch", No. 063 in a series of web material studies: a depth switch that goes from light to dark, from the sea's surface to the floor of the abyss. Build it as one self-contained page with no libraries: raw WebGL2, Web Audio and a 2D pixel buffer.

PAGE
- Editorial layout: a small kicker "Material Studies / No. 063 · WebGL + Web Audio", an italic serif title "Deep Dive Switch.", and a one-line caption.
- The switch sits centred and large. Below it go three readouts (Depth, Zone, Music), a hint line and a "Sound on/off" button.
- The whole page's colours (background, text, lines) follow the depth: pale aqua at the surface, near-black blue in the abyss.
- It must work at phone width.

THE SWITCH
- A pill-shaped switch in a moulded bezel: white glossy plastic at the surface, deep navy in the abyss.
  - A soft drop shadow falls on the page and fades to nothing before the canvas edge.
  - A slight inner shadow runs along the top of the track.
- Inside it is a 176×50 pixel-art cross-section of the sea.
  - Redraw it every frame on the CPU and show it with nearest sampling, never smoothed.
  - Use whole device pixels per scene pixel where there is room.
- The knob is a glass bathysphere: a vertical capsule of clear glass, a little taller than the track, drawn in a single full-canvas WebGL2 fragment shader.
  - It magnifies what is under it (about 1.28×) and bends it.
  - At its rim it splits R, G and B. A darker refraction band sits inside a bright edge, with a Fresnel tint and a faint aqua cast.
  - Two highlights: a long soft streak at the upper left and a small dot at the lower right.
  - Light gathers toward its foot, and it casts a soft shadow on the scene.
- Motion:
  - It follows the finger on a spring, lagging a little.
  - It stretches sideways with speed and squashes vertically to keep its volume.
  - It wobbles on a damped spring driven by its acceleration.
- Controls:
  - Drag the knob, or drag anywhere on the track.
  - Tap to send it to the other end; it travels there on its spring.
  - Arrow keys, Home/End and Space/Enter also work.
  - The switch has role="slider" with ARIA values.

THE SEA (left = shallow, right = deep; an original palette)
- Sprites are filled shapes stamped with an automatic 1-px outline and a light top / dark bottom.
- The sea floor, left to right:
  - a sandy beach with a sandcastle;
  - a reef plateau with rocks;
  - a drop-off into rocky deep water;
  - the abyssal floor rising again at the far right.
- Up top on the left is sky with a sun, two flapping gulls and a little red sailboat bobbing on animated waves with a foam line.
  - The surface is level over the shallows, then rises out of the picture toward the deep, so the view seems to sink.
- The shallows:
  - turquoise water with swaying slanted god rays and moving caustics on the sand;
  - branching corals in pink, orange and violet, brain corals, swaying sea grass;
  - an anemone with a little orange-and-white fish darting about it;
  - a sea turtle gliding back and forth, paddling;
  - a school of yellow fish circling over the reef that scatters away from the knob.
- The twilight zone:
  - the water darkens to deep blue;
  - three translucent jellyfish, pink and violet, pulse and trail wavy tentacles; they glow softly and pulse faster when the knob comes near;
  - every half minute a faint whale silhouette swims past in the background.
- The midnight zone:
  - a long swaying chain of glowing cyan-and-green beads (a siphonophore);
  - small dark lanternfish with blinking light spots;
  - marine snow drifting down.
- The abyssal floor:
  - a hydrothermal vent breathing bubbles;
  - an anglerfish with a rod and a glowing lure;
  - a treasure chest.

LIGHT AND THE DIVE
- Daylight falls off with depth and dims a little toward the floor. It is quantised and Bayer-dithered so the gradient steps like pixel art.
- Below the shallows the bathysphere's searchlight comes on: a stepped, dithered pool of light around the knob, with a blue haze scattered in the water.
- Inside the lens everything is shown lit.
- Behind the knob trail rising bubbles and, in the dark, sparks of blue bioluminescence.
- Glowing crescent echoes trail behind it: pale aqua in the shallows, cyan in the deep.
- The lure lights its own little pool.
- As the knob nears, the anglerfish turns and opens its toothy mouth wide, and its lure blazes.
- At the very bottom the chest lid swings open on glowing gold, and gold glints fly up from it.

SOUND — all synthesised live with Web Audio, original music
- 84 BPM, a four-bar loop in D minor (Dm7 · B♭maj7 · Gm7 · A7sus4), on one lookahead-scheduled clock with a little swing.
- Layers fade in and out with depth:
  0. The surface: waves (filtered noise swelling slowly) and gull cries. The moment you go under, a splash, and the waves drop to a dull underwater roar.
  1. The reef: a kalimba ostinato (sine with bright, quickly fading overtones, in a long reverb), with bubbles popping on the off-beats.
  2. A soft dub beat: a round kick, rim clicks into a dotted echo, a swung shaker, a deep bass.
  3. The twilight: slow detuned pads, a whale singing now and then (a gliding, vibrato tone through a formant filter), then sonar pings ringing in the echo.
  4. The abyss: a breathing sub drone, a slow lub-dub heartbeat, and glassy arpeggios of high pentatonic notes ringing in the echo.
- The music sits behind a gentle low-pass that closes a little with depth, about 5 dB under the switch's own sounds.
- Switch sounds:
  - a bubble bloop when grabbed, a plop when released;
  - a water swish and bubble pops that grow with drag speed;
  - a splash crossing the surface either way;
  - a glass chime past each jellyfish;
  - the angler's deep gulp;
  - a fanfare when the chest opens: a rising kalimba arpeggio, a low boom and a shimmer.
- Audio starts on the first touch; a Sound on/off button.

READOUTS
- Depth, 0 → 6,000 m, mapped to the zones.
- Zone: Surface / Sunlit / Twilight / Midnight / Abyss.
- Music: Waves / Kalimba / Reef dub / Whale song / Sonar / Abyss.

author: alliekmiller
post_text:
🚨 BREAKING: Anthropic has released Claude Fable 5.2

I tested the new model and had it build a nationwide water safety map for me.

My question was which big American cities are best set up for water in the next few decades. The #1 answer, according to the model it built out, is...

Indianapolis, Indiana.

From one prompt, it scoured federal data across the EPA, USGS, NOAA, FEMA, and the Census Bureau (more than 5 GB, including 15.5 million EPA violation records and 2 million PFAS test results). Then I had a dozen other AI agents check its work (which found some errors, like Alaska’s North Slope getting a high score because its temperature data was missing).

The final map rates 3,100 counties and more than 900 city areas on 17 measures. On an aggregate score between water supply, climate outlook, water quality, testing and oversight, and backup, Indianapolis scored the highest. Cleveland trails by about a tenth of a point, with Cincinnati, St. Louis, and Nashville right behind.
It is insane to me that I can have a research question in my head and get this level of insight hours later.
